processing: Ripe pu-erh, wet-piled and steamed, then pressed into a small tuo at Xiaguan. On FT 7513 lots, FT is the initial of Feitai Company, which commissioned the pressing according to a retailer, and 7513 the label number.
harvest_season: No specific picking is advertised; it is a recipe tea sold by production year.
appearance_dry: A small, firm, dark brown tuo, also sold packed in boxes.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown and clear, as is typical of ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaf and fragments, soft after steeping.
taste_profile: As is typical of ripe Xiaguan tuos, earthy, woody and smooth, with aged notes coming forward in older lots.

brewing.notes: Break it from the hollow side with a pick and rinse once or twice. A tight pressing needs a few steeps to open fully.

vintage_note: Sold by production year, in boxes of tuos, and aged lots such as 2010 are still on the market. As with other factory shu it can be drunk young, but several years of rest are a selling point here. Check the year and the FT 7513 number on the box.
description:
Xiao fa tuo literally means the tuo sold to France. It is a classic Xiaguan ripe pu-erh with an export story attached.

It is made as other ripe tuos are: wet-piled leaf, steamed and pressed into a small bowl. The FT 7513 code goes with it: FT stands for Feitai, the company that one retailer says commissioned the 2010 lot from Xiaguan, and 7513 is the label number. Explanations of the digits vary, so treat any neat decoding with caution.

Expect earth, wood and a smooth, low-bitterness cup, rounder with some years on it. Use very hot water, rinse well and let the tight tuo open over a few short steeps before judging it.

Buy it by year and from a trusted seller, since the name is well known. Older boxes are a reasonable way to try aged factory shu, but look at storage as much as at the date.
history:
Sellers and Chinese press date the tea to the 1970s; one Chinese media report gives 1976 and calls it the first of its kind exported to Europe, adding that it reached French pharmacies. A retailer describes it as the first pu-erh formally exported to the West, a claim best read as trade lore.

Xinhua has reported that Yunnan tuo tea shipped to France found many buyers there, which gave the tea its name. No documentation of the first batch has been traced.
